title: Saggar firing technique
subtitle: Using a saggar to protect or deliberately atmosphere pieces in an electric kiln
excerpt: A saggar is a ceramic container placed inside the kiln to protect or alter the atmosphere around pieces during firing. In traditional production ceramics, saggars protected work from flame and debris. In contemporary studio ceramics, the saggar is used offensively: loading the saggar with combustible materials (seaweed, copper wire, salt, sawdust) creates a localised reduction atmosphere inside an oxidation electric kiln, producing surface effects impossible in a standard electric firing.
sourceNotes: Saggar firing technique synthesised from contemporary studio ceramics practice for atmospheric effects in electric kilns. Traditional saggar use documented in industrial ceramics history; contemporary artistic application developed from the 1970s onward.

content.text: Kiln and firing safety

Saggar firing with combustible materials inside an electric kiln produces smoke. The kiln must be in a ventilated space or outdoors. Do not fire a saggar in an enclosed room without adequate ventilation: carbon monoxide is produced.

Copper carbonate in the saggar is toxic by inhalation. Wear an N95 mask when loading copper carbonate materials. Do not open the kiln until fully cool: copper fumes from the firing are dangerous when hot.

The combustible materials inside the saggar will smoulder and produce carbon as the temperature rises. This is expected and intentional, but the kiln must be checked periodically during firing. Have a fire extinguisher accessible.
Saggar-fired pieces are NOT food-safe unless specifically glazed with a food-safe glaze after the saggar firing. The burnished surface is decorative only.
The
saggar
creates a sealed space inside the kiln. Inside it, burning sawdust, seaweed, and copper wire build their own atmosphere: localised reduction and carbon deposition on the pieces.
Flashing
and carbon marks from this atmosphere produce results that look like wood-fire or pit-fire effects inside an otherwise controllable electric kiln.
Making or sourcing a saggar

A saggar can be thrown on the wheel from a grogged clay body. Make it a wide, low cylinder with thick walls (10 to 12 mm). The flat lid sits on the rim but does not seal completely. The small gap lets gas escape. A fully sealed saggar would burst from gas pressure. Commercial saggars in high-fire refractory clay are available from ceramic suppliers. The saggar must fit inside the kiln with at least 30 mm clearance on all sides.
Preparing the pieces
Build or throw pieces in earthenware or grogged stoneware at 6 to 8 mm wall thickness. At leather-hard,
burnish
the surface with a smooth stone or the back of a spoon. Apply terra sigillata for a finer, more reflective surface: brush on, allow to dry, burnish over the dry slip.
Allow pieces to be fully bone-dry before saggar firing. Even light residual moisture causes cracking as steam pressure builds in the first phase of heating.
Loading the saggar

Lay a bed of sawdust 3 to 4 cm deep in the base of the saggar. Place the first pieces on the sawdust, not touching each other or the saggar walls. Surround each piece with combustible materials chosen for their effect:

Sawdust and wood shavings: general carbon atmosphere, grey and black marks. Seaweed or salt-saturated material: sodium flashing, orange and cream marks. Copper wire wrapped around the piece: copper-red and green flash at contact points (wear N95 mask when loading). Banana skins: potassium flash, dark organic marks. Iron wire: red-brown flash.

Fill around the pieces with more sawdust to just below the top of the pieces. Apply kiln wash to the inside base of the saggar. Place the lid on the saggar with a deliberate gap on one side (one corner unsealed) to allow gas escape.
Firing
Fire slowly through the early stages to prevent
thermal shock
in the saggar and the pieces: 50 °C per hour from room temperature to 600 °C. After 600 °C, increase rate to 100 to 150 °C per hour to peak temperature.

Peak temperature for earthenware pieces: 950 to 1000 °C (cone 06 to cone 02). Hold at peak for 30 minutes to even out temperature across the saggar. The saggar interior reaches a slightly lower temperature than the kiln exterior due to insulation.

Allow the kiln to cool naturally with the lid down. Do not open until below 100 °C. Remove the saggar only when cool enough to handle. Open the saggar outside or in a ventilated space: residual fumes from the combustion materials may still be present.

rows.cause: Heating too fast in early stages; thermal shock to the saggar
rows.fix: Slow down the early heating rate. Never use a saggar that has hairline cracks: it will fail in the firing.

rows.problem: Pieces inside show very little surface effect: just uniform grey
rows.cause: Too much sawdust, not enough varied materials; or gap in saggar lid too large (too much oxygen)
rows.fix: Pack varied materials around pieces. Reduce the gap in the lid: it should be small enough to restrict oxygen, not open.

rows.problem: Copper flash is green, not red
rows.cause: Kiln atmosphere reached the pieces as oxidation rather than reduction; copper wire burned in oxidation
rows.fix: Seal the saggar lid more tightly. Pack more combustible material around the copper wire pieces.
